title: Split a big sum with fork/join

task.text: Implement `SumTask.compute()`: sum an `int[]` range by splitting it until the pieces are small.

items: `SumTask(int[] data, int from, int to, int threshold)` sums `data[from, to)` as a `long`; the constructor is given.
A range of at most `threshold` elements is summed directly in a loop. Call `onLeaf.accept(from, to)` just before, and keep that hook.
A larger range is cut at the middle into two `SumTask`s: fork one, compute the other yourself, then join.
Do not create threads, executors or streams: the caller supplies the `ForkJoinPool`.

checks.title: Empty, tiny and offset ranges sum correctly
The sum is accumulated as a long
A million elements match a plain loop
Direct sums cover the range exactly
Two halves really run in parallel
compute splits with fork and join
The task brings no threads of its own

hints.text: Fork/join is divide and conquer with a cutoff: below the threshold a plain loop is cheaper than scheduling, above it the range splits in two independent halves. Decide the base case first.
In the recursive case build two `SumTask`s for `[from, mid)` and `[mid, to)`. Fork one so another worker can steal it, compute the other directly on this thread, and only then join the forked one.

lines: var left = new SumTask(data, from, mid, threshold);
var right = new SumTask(data, mid, to, threshold);
